prompt: You press Ctrl+T on the `Sales` data and Excel proposes `=$A$1:$J$109`. What does that tell you?
hint: The data ends in column H.

choices.text: Excel always adds two spare columns to a new table
choices.why: It proposes the block of filled cells around the one you clicked, and nothing more.

choices.text: A forgotten helper cell is touching the data
choices.why: Right. Cancel, delete it, and Excel will propose A1:H109.

choices.text: The headers of the table are in column J
choices.why: The headers are in row 1; J is simply part of what Excel found filled.

choices.text: Nothing: a wider table holds the same data and costs nothing
choices.why: Columns I and J would become table columns, and every lesson after this one expects eight.

prompt: You type `=[@Bags]*[@Price]` in H2 of the `Sales` table. What is the column now?
hint: What does a new row get?

choices.text: A column of 108 separate formulas, each one adjusted to its own row
choices.why: That is what lesson 2's =E2*F2 filled down was. In a table every row holds the same text.

choices.text: A calculated column: one formula for the column, which a new row receives by itself
choices.why: Right, which is why H110 shows 636 the moment a sale is typed on row 110.

choices.text: A column of values, since tables do not keep formulas
choices.why: Tables keep formulas; they keep one per column.

choices.text: A column that only the total row can read
choices.why: Any formula can read Sales[Revenue], on any sheet.

prompt: Which of these will Excel accept as the name of a table?
hint: No spaces, and nothing that could be a cell address.

choices.text: Sales 2025
choices.why: Table names cannot contain spaces.

choices.text: S1
choices.why: S1 is a cell address, so Excel refuses it as a name.

choices.text: 2025-Sales
choices.why: A table name has to start with a letter or an underscore, and the hyphen is not allowed either.

choices.text: Sales
choices.why: Right, and it is the name every later lesson uses.

prompt: Inside a table, `[@Bags]` stands for the value of the `Bags` column on the formula's own ___.
hint: Horizontal, not vertical.

prompt: What does `=ROWS(Sales[Sale])` answer once the table is made?
hint: Data rows only, never the header.

prompt: On the `Report` sheet, `=SUM(Sales[Bags])` works with no sheet name in front of it. Why?
hint: Who does a table belong to?

choices.text: Excel guesses the sheet from the column name
choices.why: There is nothing to guess: the name Sales is unique in the workbook.

choices.text: A table belongs to the workbook, so its name is found from any sheet
choices.why: Right, unlike Sales!E2:E109, which needs the sheet.

choices.text: The table and the sheet are both called Sales, which Excel requires
choices.why: They need not share a name; the course chose it for clarity.

choices.text: It only works on sheets created after the table
choices.why: It works on every sheet of the workbook, old or new.

prompt: You drag B3's formula, which uses `Sales[Bags]`, to the right with the fill handle, and C3 now reads `Sales[Price]`. What keeps the column fixed?
hint: Dragging moves table columns the way it moves letters.

choices.text: Put a $ in front: $Sales[Bags]
choices.why: A $ does nothing to a structured reference; that syntax is not a table reference at all.

choices.text: Nothing can: structured references always move
choices.why: They move only when dragged. Copying keeps them, and a column range fixes them.

choices.text: Copy and paste the cell, or write Sales[[Bags]:[Bags]]
choices.why: Right. Pasting keeps table references, and the column range stays put however it is filled.

choices.text: Convert the table back to a range first
choices.why: That throws away the names, which were the point.

prompt: Match each reference to what it covers in the `Sales` table.
hint: The table in the section.

pairs.right: The data rows of one column
One column's value on the formula's own row
Headers, data and total row together

prompt: With sale S1109 typed on row 110, what does `=SUM(Sales[Bags])` answer?
hint: The 591 of the course, plus the new sale.

prompt: With S1109 on row 110, `=SUM(E2:E109)` still answers 591. Why?
hint: What does an address know about the table?

choices.text: Excel recalculates addresses only when the file is saved
choices.why: It recalculated; the answer is right for the cells it names.

choices.text: An address stops where it was written, and row 110 is outside it
choices.why: Right, and no error says so. The table name grew with the table.

choices.text: Row 110 is a total row, which SUM skips
choices.why: It is a sale; the total row is off.

choices.text: The new sale's bags were typed as text
choices.why: They were typed as the number 6; the table's own total counts them.

prompt: You type a sale in A111, leaving row 110 empty. What happens to the table?
hint: Which row can a table grow into?

choices.text: The table grows to row 111 and leaves 110 as an empty sale
choices.why: It grows only into the row that touches it.

choices.text: Excel moves the sale up to row 110
choices.why: Excel never moves what you typed.

choices.text: Nothing joins: the sale sits outside the table, and no formula naming it counts the sale
choices.why: Right. Delete the gap, or type the sale on row 110.

choices.text: The table is converted back into a range
choices.why: Typing near a table never undoes it.

prompt: Put the section's test of a growing table in order.
hint: Add, check, remove, check.
items: Click A110, under the last sale
Type S1109 across the row, with Tab between cells
Delete the row with Delete › Table Rows
trap: Skipping the last check leaves a sale that is not the course's in every total from here on.

prompt: You choose Sum in the total row under `Bags`. What formula does the cell hold?
hint: The total row writes the same function for every item of its list.

choices.text: =SUM([Bags])
choices.why: SUM would add hidden rows too; the total row uses a function that follows the filter.

choices.text: =SUBTOTAL(109,[Bags])
choices.why: Right. 109 means sum, leaving out what a filter or a hand hides.

choices.text: =SUMIFS([Bags], [Channel], "*")
choices.why: A condition that every row passes; the total row writes nothing like it.

choices.text: =TOTAL(Sales[Bags])
choices.why: There is no TOTAL function in Excel.

prompt: With the table filtered to `Wholesale`, what does `=SUBTOTAL(103, Sales[Sale])` answer?
hint: 103 counts the visible cells that are not empty.

prompt: Filtered to `Wholesale`, the total row shows 403 bags, while `=SUM(Sales[Bags])` in another cell shows 591. Why do they differ?
hint: One function looks at what is on screen.

choices.text: SUM is out of date until the sheet is recalculated
choices.why: Both are current. They answer different questions.

choices.text: SUM adds every row of the column; SUBTOTAL leaves out the rows the filter hides
choices.why: Right. One counts the column, the other counts the screen.

choices.text: The total row counts the wholesale rows twice
choices.why: 403 is exactly the wholesale bags, as SUMIFS confirmed in lesson 5.

choices.text: SUM cannot read a structured reference while a filter is on
choices.why: It reads it; it simply does not care about the filter.

prompt: On the filtered table, `SUBTOTAL(9, …)` and `SUBTOTAL(109, …)` give the same 403. When would they differ?
hint: Two ways a row can be out of sight.

choices.text: When the table has more than 109 rows
choices.why: The number picks the calculation, not a row limit.

choices.text: When somebody also hides a row by hand
choices.why: Right: 9 still adds rows hidden by hand, 109 leaves them out. Both leave out filtered rows.

choices.text: When the filter is cleared
choices.why: With nothing hidden, both add every row and agree again.

choices.text: Never: 9 is only the old spelling of 109
choices.why: They are two families, and they treat hand-hidden rows differently.

prompt: Your manager wants the wholesale bags in a monthly report. Where should the number come from?
hint: Which one still says wholesale after the filter is cleared?

choices.text: The total row, filtered to Wholesale, copied into the report
choices.why: The copy carries 403 and not the filter, so the next reader cannot tell what it counts.

choices.text: A SUMIFS that names its condition
choices.why: Right: the formula carries the condition with it. Use the total row to look, and SUMIFS to keep.

choices.text: A SUM over the visible cells, selected by hand
choices.why: That is a filter you have to remember, done again every month.

choices.text: The status bar at the bottom of the window
choices.why: It shows the selection's sum and leaves nothing behind to check.

prompt: With the `Cost` column filled, what does `=SUM(Sales[Cost])` answer?
hint: Bags times today's unit cost, over all 108 sales.

prompt: After a `Supplier` column is inserted before `Grams` in `Products`, `=VLOOKUP([@Product], Products, 7, FALSE)` answers 118 on row 2, while the `Cost` column is unchanged. Why?
hint: What does each formula use to find the column it returns?

choices.text: The 7 now counts to List price; XLOOKUP names Products[Unit cost]
choices.why: Right. A position moves when columns do; a name does not.

choices.text: VLOOKUP cannot read a table that has more than seven columns
choices.why: It reads any width; it returns whatever sits in seventh place.

choices.text: The insert changed the price of CER1K to 118
choices.why: 118 was always CER1K's list price; the VLOOKUP now reads that column instead of Unit cost.

choices.text: FALSE should be TRUE once a table has grown
choices.why: TRUE would ask for an approximate match, which lesson 4 warns about; it does not fix the column.

prompt: The lesson computes a gross margin of R$ 21,104 and calls it an estimate. Why?
hint: When was each bag roasted, and at what cost?

choices.text: Lookups between tables round every value
choices.why: The lookup returns the unit cost exactly.

choices.text: The margin leaves out the shop sales
choices.why: It covers all 108 sales, every channel.

choices.text: Unit cost holds today's cost, and the 2025 bags cost whatever they cost then
choices.why: Right. The tables do not record the cost at the time of each sale.

choices.text: Revenue includes the 2026 price rise twice
choices.why: Revenue is what was paid, sale by sale; nothing is counted twice.

prompt: How did the `Cost` column become part of the `Sales` table?
hint: Section 04: a table grows in two directions.

choices.text: By typing a header in the first empty column beside the table
choices.why: Right. The table takes the column in, and the formula typed under it becomes a calculated column.

choices.text: By recreating the table with Ctrl+T over A1:I109
choices.why: No need: a table grows sideways by itself.

choices.text: By choosing Insert › Table Columns on the Sales sheet
choices.why: That inserts a column inside the table; typing beside it is how the lesson adds one at the end.

choices.text: By naming the column Cost in the Name Manager
choices.why: Column names are the headers, typed in the header row.

prompt: Next month's sales are pasted directly under the `Sales` table. Which of these formulas include them without being edited? Choose all that apply.
hint: Which ones name the table?

choices.text: `=SUM(Sales[Bags])`
choices.why: It names the column of the table, which grows with the paste.
The address still ends at row 109.

choices.text: `=SUMIFS(Sales[Revenue], Sales[Channel], "Online")`
choices.why: Both ranges are table columns, so both grow.

choices.text: `=COUNTIFS(G2:G109, "Online")`
choices.why: An address again: the new rows are below it.

choices.text: `=ROWS(Sales[Sale])`
choices.why: It counts the table's rows, whatever they are.

prompt: What is the average revenue per wholesale sale? Use `AVERAGEIFS` with structured references, and give it to two decimal places.
hint: Average the Revenue column where Channel is Wholesale.

prompt: A student forgot to delete S1109 and goes on to lesson 10. What happens to their numbers?
hint: Which formulas follow the table?

choices.text: Nothing, because lesson 10 works from the original file
choices.why: Lesson 10 builds on this workbook's tables.

choices.text: Excel refuses to build anything on a table with 109 rows
choices.why: Excel builds on any table; the trouble is that the numbers are not the course's.

choices.text: Only formulas written with addresses change
choices.why: The reverse: addresses stop at row 109, and everything that names the table includes S1109.

choices.text: Every total built on the table has six more bags and R$ 636 more revenue than the course
choices.why: Right, and comparing with the course's numbers is how they would find out.
